newsitem.title: USA: Dollar ends lower on negative Japanese comment.
newsitem.headline: Dollar ends lower on negative Japanese comment.

text.p: The dollar ended lower against major currencies Monday after a Japanese official warned his country would not tolerate "excessive" moves in the foreign exchange markets.
During overnight trade, Japan's first official session of 1997, the dollar posted a near four-year high just below 117 Japanese yen, continuing a sharp rally from the previous week.
But Japan's Vice Finance Minister Tadashi Ogawa subsequently prompted heavy sales of dollars for yen, saying the government would "deal appropriately" with excessive foreign exchange shifts.
That suggested Japanese monetary authorities might at some point enter the market to buy yen for dollars if the yen continues to slide, currency experts said.

"The dollar came off overnight following the Ogawa comment. He basically said excessive yen depreciation is not necessarily what they're looking for," said John McCarthy, senior vice president for foreign exchange at ING Barings.
The dollar ended at 115.72 yen, down from 116.33 late Friday and a high of 116.95 early in the session.

The U.S. currency also posted early gains versus the mark, breaching 1.57 and nearly posting a two-year high. But the dollar's weakness against the yen eventually helped drag it lower against European currencies, dealers said.
The dollar fell to 1.5637 marks from 1.5660 late Friday.

"We had to wait until U.S. trading got underway before the Ogawa news caught up to the dollar and it gave up some ground to the mark," said Elliott Dix, foreign exchange trader at Signet Bank in Richmond, Va.
Most traders still see the dollar continuing its recent rally, despite Monday's setback, moving gradually toward 120 yen and 1.57 marks in coming sessions.
"Frankly, most people are bullish here. It's hard not to be," said James Powers, corporate foreign exchange vice president at Westdeutsche Landesbank Girozentrale in New York.
The British pound traded erratically, rising toward $1.70 in early trade before selling off sharply to below $1.68. Sterling ultimately settled at $1.6930, up from $1.6877 late Friday.
"Sterling had a tricky kind of day. There was a lot of movement," Powers said.
In other trading, the dollar fell to 1.3533 Swiss francs from 1.3595 on Friday and to Canadian $1.3648 from C$1.3700.
